newsitem.title: CHINA: China acceptance of IMF condition helps investors.
newsitem.headline: China acceptance of IMF condition helps investors.

text.p: China's acceptance of the IMF's Article VIII on currency convertibility is an important step forward giving foreign investors greater security, an IMF representative and analysts said on Monday.

The Chinese government told the International Monetary Fund late last month that it would acceed to Article VIII from December 1, thereby committing itself to a new level of openness on currency transactions.

Article VIII requires countries to refrain from imposing restrictions on the payment of funds for transfers for current international transactions, or from engaging in discriminatory currency arrangements.
China announced that the yuan was convertible on the current account from December 1.

"This is an important symbolic step for China," said Jonathan Anderson, the IMF's deputy representative to China. "It provides an additional safeguard to foreign investors, who can assume that, for instance, China will not increase restrictions on transfer of profits."
There are still restrictions on the amount of local money Chinese people can change for foreign currency -- a maximum of $1,000 is allowed for each citizen travelling abroad under the current rules.
But Anderson, speaking by telephone from Beijing, said the IMF had received assurances from China that this would be treated with flexibility in the future.
"They are now referring to this as an 'indicative limit', and that if people provide the necessary documentation, greater amounts will be allowable," he said.

A foreign banker in Shanghai said China's announcement of convertibility on the current account was significantly faster than many people had expected, although the procedures for money conversion still involved a lot of bureaucracy.
"It was way of ahead of the original schedule. They had talked before about achieving current account convertibility by the year 2000. That's an achievement," the banker said.
"In terms of the documents required, it still a hassle, but at the end of the day they are really doing what they claim," he added.

Convertibility on the capital account, effectively moving the yuan to full convertibility, was still many years away, possibly 15 or more, said Economics Professor Huang Zemin of the East China Normal University.
"In Japan, the shift from convertibility on the current account to the capital account took 20 years from 1964 to 1984," Huang said in an interview.
"Given China's situation it should be similar, although given the speed with which the Chinese economy is growing it may be a bit faster," he added.

The IMF's Anderson said the Chinese authorities had been careful not to give any timetable on the shift to convertibility on the capital account, but said he felt they understood the fundamental value of making the change.
"It would result in a more rational use of economic funds. In the short term, there may be some outflow of capital, but, in the long term, it should give rise to greater inflows," he said.
